title: Yayati and the seasons of a life
hookLine: Yayati borrows his son's youth and learns that each aim of life has its season.
carry: each aim of life has its season
tomorrow: a book about desire draws its own family tree. who's in it?
last: A DESTINED SEED STILL NEEDS PLANTING.

cards: King Yayati, in the Mahabharata, is cursed with old age too soon. He may pass it to one of his sons, if one will take it. Only the youngest, Puru, agrees, and gives his father his youth.
For a thousand years, the story says, Yayati enjoys every pleasure. Then he gives the youth back. Desire, he says, is never quenched by enjoying it; it only grows, like a fire fed with ghee.
He crowns Puru and goes to the forest.

teach.h: THE ASHRAMAS: SEASONS OF A LIFE.
teach.b: Hindu teaching gives the aims of life seasons, and the ashramas, the stages of life, carry them: the student, the householder, the one who steps back, the one who renounces.
The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter gives its own version. In childhood, learning.

teach.h: LEARNING, LOVE AND LIVING, THEN DHARMA.
teach.b: In youth and the middle years, artha and kama, a living and love. In old age, dharma, and the search for moksha, release. The aims take turns, so none crowds out the rest.

Yayati tried to stretch one season forever, and found the fire only grew. Then the chapter admits a catch: life is uncertain, so a person may practice each aim as its moment comes, not only on schedule.
One thing it won't bend on: the years of study come first.
Now hold up the week. Arjuna answering the cry at the gate. Ravana letting one aim swallow the rest.
A butcher teaching a scholar the dharma for all. Kama burned, and still a rightful aim.

Kichaka turning the order upside down. Savitri meeting fate with effort. Two very different books, and the old stories around them, working on one question: how dharma, artha, kama and moksha share one human life.

how: Hindu teaching often pairs the aims of life with the ashramas, the stages of life, from student to householder to later years of stepping back; the Kama Sutra's opening gives its own version, and Yayati's story is the classic warning against clinging to one season.

games.q: what does “the kama sutra's ethics chapter” mean?
o: the part of a well-known old book that sets a king's daily hours
the part of a well-known old book that lists festival seasons
the part of a well-known old book that gives life's aims seasons

games.q: the seasons of a life — tap the pairs.
p: dharma, and the search for moksha

s: the chapter says each aim must wait for its exact season
it sketches seasons, then says life is uncertain, so each aim can be practiced as its moment comes.
it places dharma and the search for moksha in old age
learning first, then a living and love, then dharma and release.
it lets study be squeezed in around everything else
the years of study come first, and stay focused until they're done.

games.q: your grandfather is 78. he still spends every weekend chasing one more business deal and says temple and the Gita can wait till 'later'. by the chapter and Yayati's story, what fits?
o: his season has turned toward dharma and moksha; Yayati found more never fills you.
keep chasing. artha is chief, at every age.
he was wrong to work at all. artha is a lesser aim.
games.why: the chapter gives old age to dharma and the search for moksha, and Yayati found desire fed only grows. and since life is uncertain, 'later' is the riskiest plan of all.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable. On each slow breath, let one season of your own life come to mind, one past, the one you're in, one still ahead, and simply notice which aim has filled it.
Rest on the season you're in for the last few breaths. If you pray, close by saying a name of God you love, once. If you don't, close with a quiet thank you for this season.

wordCard.voice: The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter: the aims in seasons, learning, then a living and love, then dharma and moksha, each in its moment.

orig.note: Sanskrit moksha, release: in the chapter's plan, sought in old age alongside dharma.

carryVoice: Your line: each aim of life has its season. Yayati found the fire only grows. That's a week.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Yayati takes his son Puru's youth, then returns it: desire is never quenched by enjoyment but grows like fire fed with ghee; the same verse appears as Manusmriti 2.94)
Kama Sutra 1.2 (the aims by stage of life; practice as occasion allows since life is uncertain; studentship first)
